title: Milk and honey on Broadway and black performers
summary: Nightclub shows moved into theatres, helping black performers get work in interracial shows until the battle of the bands.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: So what was it like on Broadway at that time?
Well, it was milk and honey at that time. Especially for show business, because they began to move the

nightclub shows into theaters also. And that was because it was better increases in pay. Everyone's finances began to improve. And they kept it up until -- right up until the early '40s, see, and they went out with the battle of bands. That's how it went out, began to let up, you know. When they didn't have so many shows, wasn't so active.
Would you say it was milk and honey for the black performer or for all performers?
Was black in at that time?

Yeah. Well, that's why I said it was particularly for the blacks. See, the blacks wasn't as plentiful as the whites. But I mean, just to be appearing in an interracial show, like -- (recording interruption) So it was particularly an advantage and a great improvement for the blacks because they began to work also in the theaters from nightclubs, and then it went on up to around in the early -- till the battle of bands, and Benny Goodman became King of Swing, went into that, went out with the battle of bands, but they still continued variety shows.
